title: Molecular Dynamics-Derived Coloured Noise Mediates Anderson Localisation and Environment-Assisted Transport of Tryptophan Excitons in Tubulin
abstract: The tryptophan residues in tubulin $αβ$-dimers form an ordered aromatic network that has been proposed to support quantum exciton transport even under physiological environmental noise. Existing studies of this system mostly assume white-noise dephasing, but the statistical properties of the protein-solvent bath coupled to tryptophan sites remain uncharacterised under physiological conditions. Here we characterise this fluctuation bath via all-atom molecular dynamics simulations of a solvated tubulin dimer at 310~K, combining high-frequency and long-time trajectories with 10~fs and 10~ps sampling intervals. The resulting autocorrelation of the site-energy fluctuations is tri-exponential, with three well-separated decay modes: sub-100-fs and picosecond fluctuations driven by water dynamics, and a nanosecond mode originating from protein conformational rearrangements. All three modes fall deep within the non-Markovian regime. We further demonstrate that the slow protein mode introduces strong quasi-static disorder, which results in Anderson localisation, while the two fast water modes frequently tune chromophore pairs through resonance, enabling environment-assisted quantum transport (ENAQT). On the full eight-site network, the coloured-noise bath confines excitons predominantly to strongly coupled proximal tryptophan pairs, in marked contrast to the more uniform delocalisation predicted by the standard white-noise Haken--Strobl model. Our workflow generalises to other pigment--protein systems with solvent-exposed chromophores.
summary: This work develops a detailed model for exciton transport in protein chromophores by deriving the environmental noise spectrum directly from all-atom MD simulations. The analysis reveals that the multi-timescale colored noise leads to Anderson localization, confining excitons to specific pairs rather than allowing uniform delocalization. This methodology is valuable for understanding quantum processes in complex biological environments.
main_problem: The study aims to characterize quantum exciton transport in a protein's tryptophan network under realistic, non-Markovian environmental noise conditions.
main_result: The colored noise bath causes excitons to localize predominantly on strongly coupled proximal pairs via Anderson localization, contrasting with predictions from simple white-noise models.
method: All-atom Molecular Dynamics (MD) simulations are used to derive the time-dependent site-energy fluctuations ($\delta\epsilon_m(t)$), which are then incorporated into a stochastic Schrödinger equation solved using colored noise modeling.
model_or_system: The system is an eight-site network of tryptophan residues within tubulin $\alpha eta$-dimers. The exciton dynamics are governed by a Hamiltonian whose site energies fluctuate due to the protein/solvent environment, modeled as a superposition of three Ornstein–Uhlenbeck processes.
key_observables: Site-energy autocorrelation function (tri-exponential), Participation Ratio ($PR$), and localization length.
important_parameters: Three distinct noise timescales: sub-100-fs (water), picosecond (water), and nanosecond (protein conformational rearrangements).
main_assumptions: The bath dynamics are modeled as a superposition of three independent Ornstein–Uhlenbeck processes, assuming the system operates deep within the non-Markovian regime.
figures_summary: Figures illustrate dipole geometries, site-energy fluctuation traces comparing short vs. long trajectories, and eigenstate localization plots showing confinement under disorder.
paper_structure: The paper first characterizes the multi-timescale nature of environmental fluctuations using MD simulations, then models the exciton dynamics using a colored-noise Hamiltonian, and finally analyzes how this complex noise leads to specific localization patterns versus simple delocalization.
why_interesting: It provides a rigorous framework for modeling open quantum systems where the bath correlation time is explicitly derived from molecular simulation, moving beyond simplified Markovian assumptions common in bio-physics.
